title: Learn JavaScript on Your Phone: The Complete HirenJS Community Guide (2026)
excerpt: Want to learn JavaScript on your phone with no laptop? This free beginner guide covers setup, a 12-week roadmap, practice projects, debugging tips and how to get help.
author: Hiren Rathod
content:
If you have ever typed "learn JavaScript on your phone" into a search bar late at night, half hoping for a yes and half expecting someone to tell you to buy a laptop first, this post is for you. The short answer is yes. You can learn JavaScript on your phone, you can start today without installing anything, and you can get genuinely good at it if you practise in the right way.

I'm Hiren, and I built HirenJS for exactly this situation. Not for people with a fast laptop and a second monitor, but for students whose only computer fits in a pocket. This is the first big community guide on the blog, and it's the one I wish somebody had handed me when I was starting out. It covers what to learn, in what order, how to practise on a small screen, which mistakes make people quit in week two, and how the HirenJS community can help each other along the way.

It's long on purpose. Bookmark it, read one section a day, and come back whenever you feel stuck. Today is 7 October 2026, which is as good a day as any to begin.

In This Guide

  • Can you really learn JavaScript on a phone?
  • What HirenJS is and who it's for
  • Setting up your phone for mobile coding
  • A 12-week JavaScript roadmap for beginners
  • A daily practice routine that fits a busy life
  • Seven projects you can build without a laptop
  • Common mistakes and how to avoid them
  • How to debug JavaScript on a smartphone
  • How to ask for help so people actually answer
  • Being part of the HirenJS community
  • What's next, plus a short FAQ

Can You Really Learn JavaScript on a Phone?

Let's deal with the biggest doubt first. JavaScript is the one programming language that every phone already understands. Your browser, whether it's Chrome, Firefox, Samsung Internet or anything else, contains a JavaScript engine. That means the device in your hand is already a machine that runs JavaScript. You don't need to install a compiler, set up a virtual environment, or fight with a path variable. You open a page, type code, press Run, and something happens.

That's a huge advantage for beginners. A lot of people give up on programming before they write a single useful line, because the setup was too confusing. With a browser-based JavaScript playground, the setup is nothing at all.

Now, let me be honest about the downsides, because pretending they don't exist helps nobody. Typing on glass is slower than typing on a keyboard. The screen is small, so you see fewer lines at once. Browser developer tools are awkward on a phone. Brackets and quotes take extra taps. If you plan to build a big production application, you'll eventually want a proper keyboard and a bigger display.

But here's the thing that surprises most people: those limits barely matter in the first few months. A beginner's programs are short. You're writing five lines, then ten, then maybe thirty. You're learning ideas like variables, loops and functions, and these ideas live in your head, not in your hardware. The real bottleneck for a new learner is never the device. It's attention, consistency and having someone explain things clearly.

There's also a quiet benefit to coding on a small screen. Because you can't see much at once, you naturally write short, focused snippets and test them often. That's exactly the habit professional developers try to build. Write a little, run it, check the output, repeat. Phones push you into that rhythm whether you like it or not.

So if your situation is "I have a smartphone, patchy time, and a strong wish to learn," you're closer to being a JavaScript developer than you think. Let's make the most of it.

What HirenJS Is and Who It's For

HirenJS is a dark-themed JavaScript playground and learning site designed around smartphones. It lives at hiren.js.org, and the whole idea is simple: if a student can open a web page, they should be able to write and run JavaScript on it.

Here's what you'll find when you open it.

The editor

The editor is built on Ace, the same kind of code editor engine used in many online tools. It gives you syntax highlighting, automatic indentation, bracket matching and a clean dark interface that's gentle on your eyes during long sessions. You can cycle through six themes: One Dark, Monokai, Dracula, GitHub, Night Bright and Cobalt. Pick whichever makes the text easiest to read in your lighting.

The mobile toolbar

On phones, the five actions you use most live in a fixed bar at the bottom of the screen: Run, Undo, Clear, Format and Theme. The Run button is deliberately big and yellow so you can hit it with a thumb without squinting. On a desktop or with a Bluetooth keyboard, Ctrl+Enter does the same job.

Snippet library

Typing boilerplate on a phone keyboard is tiring, so HirenJS has a built-in snippet library. Open it, search for the pattern you want, and the code lands in your editor. The snippets are written to teach a concept rather than just fill space, so reading them is a mini lesson in itself.

HTML preview

Switch the editor to HTML mode and you get a live preview of your page in a sandboxed frame. This is where JavaScript starts to feel real, because you can make buttons respond, change text on the page and see colours update. No separate editor, no file management.

Share by link and auto-save

The Share button packs your code into a URL. Anyone with the link can open it and see exactly what you wrote, with no account and no login. That's perfect for sending a problem to a friend or a teacher. Your work is also saved automatically in your browser as you type, so closing the tab doesn't wipe it out.

Docs, quizzes and this blog

Beyond the playground, HirenJS has documentation with interactive quizzes so you can test yourself after reading, and a blog where tutorials and community updates live. If you've already read our posts on closures, array methods, async/await and scope, you've seen the style: plain language, runnable examples, no unnecessary jargon.

Who is it for? School and college students who only have a phone. Self-learners who want to try JavaScript before committing to anything bigger. Teachers who need something students can open instantly in a classroom or at home. And honestly, anyone who just wants a quick scratchpad to test an idea.

Setting Up Your Phone for Mobile Coding

You don't need to buy anything, but a few minutes of setup will make your mobile coding sessions much smoother. These are the changes I'd make before writing a single line.

Turn off autocorrect and auto-capitalisation

This is the single most useful tweak, and almost nobody tells beginners about it. Phone keyboards love to "fix" your text. They capitalise the first letter of a line, swap straight quotes for curly ones, and replace words they think you meant. In normal chatting that's helpful. In code it's a disaster, because JavaScript will not accept curly quotes, and Console.log is not the same as console.log.

Go into your keyboard settings and switch off auto-capitalisation, auto-correction, and smart punctuation. If your keyboard has a "code" or "programming" layout, or a long-press menu for symbols, get familiar with it. You'll be typing curly braces, square brackets, backticks and semicolons all the time.

Use landscape for writing, portrait for reading

Rotate your phone sideways when you're typing. You get a wider editor and more of each line on screen. Switch back to portrait when you want to read the output or a long explanation. It sounds trivial, but it changes the whole experience.

Keep your browser updated

A recent browser means the latest JavaScript features work properly and the editor runs smoothly. If an example behaves strangely, an outdated browser is a surprisingly common cause.

Close the noise

A notification in the middle of a thought can cost you ten minutes of focus. Use Do Not Disturb for your study block. Even twenty minutes of uninterrupted practice beats an hour of distracted scrolling between messages.

Keep a notes app open for questions

When something confuses you, write the question down instead of abandoning the session. "Why does this print undefined?" is a perfectly good note. You can come back to it, search for it, or bring it to the community later.

Consider a cheap Bluetooth keyboard

This is optional, but if you can get a basic Bluetooth keyboard, pairing it with your phone transforms the experience. Your typing speed jumps, shortcuts like Ctrl+Enter start working, and the on-screen keyboard stops covering half your editor. You can learn without one, but it's the best upgrade for the money.

Save your work outside the browser

Auto-save is convenient, but browsers can clear stored data, especially when storage runs low or you clean up your phone. For anything you care about, press Share, copy the link and paste it into your notes app. That link is a backup that survives almost anything.

A 12-Week JavaScript Roadmap for Beginners

Most people don't fail at learning JavaScript because it's too hard. They fail because they don't know what to learn next, so they bounce between videos and never build depth. A roadmap fixes that. The plan below assumes about 20 to 30 minutes a day, five or six days a week. If you have less time, stretch each stage. If you have more, go faster. The order is what matters.

Weeks 1 and 2: Variables, data types and printing output

Your first goal is simply to get comfortable making the computer show you things. You'll learn console.log, how to store values in variables, and the basic data types: strings, numbers, booleans, null and undefined. You'll also meet operators and template strings.

const name = 'Asha';
let age = 17;
const isStudent = true;

console.log('Name:', name);
console.log(`Next year ${name} will be ${age + 1}.`);
console.log(typeof age);       // number
console.log(typeof isStudent); // boolean

// Strings have handy built-in methods
console.log(name.toUpperCase()); // ASHA
console.log(name.length);        // 4

Spend these two weeks playing. Change values, break things on purpose, and read the error messages. Don't rush. A solid grip on const versus let now saves you a lot of confusion later. A simple rule: use const by default, switch to let only when the value needs to change, and leave var alone.

Weeks 3 and 4: Decisions and loops

Programs become interesting when they can choose and repeat. This stage covers if, else, comparison operators, logical operators like && and ||, and the for and while loops.

const marks = 72;

if (marks >= 90) {
  console.log('Grade A+');
} else if (marks >= 60) {
  console.log('Grade B');
} else {
  console.log('Keep practising!');
}

// A multiplication table
for (let i = 1; i <= 10; i++) {
  console.log(`7 x ${i} = ${7 * i}`);
}

A good exercise here is the classic FizzBuzz: print the numbers from 1 to 30, but print "Fizz" for multiples of three, "Buzz" for multiples of five, and "FizzBuzz" for both. It's small, it's a little tricky, and solving it on your own feels fantastic.

Weeks 5 and 6: Functions and scope

Functions are how you stop repeating yourself. You'll learn to declare them, pass in parameters, return values, and write the shorter arrow function style. You'll also start to understand scope, meaning where a variable can and can't be seen.

function add(a, b) {
  return a + b;
}

const square = n => n * n;

console.log(add(5, 7));   // 12
console.log(square(9));   // 81

function greet(name = 'friend') {
  return `Hello, ${name}!`;
}
console.log(greet());        // Hello, friend!
console.log(greet('Hiren')); // Hello, Hiren!

Once functions feel natural, read our posts on JavaScript scope (let, const, var and the temporal dead zone) and on closures. They go deeper than a beginner roadmap can, and they'll make sense because you've already written real functions.

Weeks 7 and 8: Arrays and objects

Almost every real program deals with collections of things: a list of students, a cart of items, a set of messages. Arrays hold ordered lists. Objects hold named properties. Together they let you model almost anything.

const student = {
  name: 'Rahul',
  scores: [85, 91, 78]
};

const total = student.scores.reduce((sum, s) => sum + s, 0);
const average = total / student.scores.length;

console.log(`${student.name}'s average is ${average.toFixed(1)}`);

const passed = student.scores.filter(s => s >= 80);
console.log(passed); // [85, 91]

This is the right moment for our guide to the top 10 array methods. Learn map, filter and reduce properly and you'll write shorter, cleaner code for the rest of your career. Try rewriting an older for loop using one of them. That small exercise teaches more than reading three articles.

Weeks 9 and 10: The DOM and your first interactive page

Until now, your code has printed text to a console. This stage is where it starts changing a real page. The DOM, short for Document Object Model, is how JavaScript sees and edits the elements on a web page. Use HirenJS in HTML mode so you can see results in the preview.

<button id="btn">Tap me</button>
<p id="out">Nothing yet.</p>

<script>
  let taps = 0;
  const btn = document.getElementById('btn');
  const out = document.getElementById('out');

  btn.addEventListener('click', () => {
    taps++;
    out.textContent = `You tapped ${taps} time${taps === 1 ? '' : 's'}.`;
  });
</script>

Notice how the pieces from earlier weeks all show up: a variable, a function, a condition, a template string. Nothing here is brand new. It's the same toolbox pointed at a different target. Play with it. Change the text, add a second button, make something turn red after five taps.

Weeks 11 and 12: Asynchronous JavaScript and a small project

The last stage introduces code that waits: timers, and fetching data from the internet. This is where many learners hit a wall, so take it slowly and read the async/await guide on this blog before you start.

async function showJoke() {
  try {
    const res = await fetch(
      'https://v2.jokeapi.dev/joke/Programming?type=single'
    );
    const data = await res.json();
    console.log(data.joke);
  } catch (err) {
    console.error('Could not load a joke:', err);
  }
}

showJoke();

Then spend the final fortnight building one small project from start to finish. Not a tutorial copy, but something you chose. The next sections give you plenty of ideas. Finishing even a tiny project teaches you more about planning, debugging and persistence than another month of passive learning.

A Daily Practice Routine That Fits a Busy Life

Consistency beats intensity. Learners who do twenty focused minutes every day nearly always overtake learners who do a five-hour burst on Sunday and nothing for the rest of the week. Your brain builds skills during the gaps between sessions, so daily contact matters.

Here's a simple template you can adapt. It fits into a single twenty-minute window, like a bus ride or the quiet time before dinner.

  • Minutes 1 to 5, recall. Without looking anything up, retype a small snippet from yesterday. A loop, a function, an array method. If you can't, that tells you what to revisit.
  • Minutes 6 to 15, new material. Read one short section of the docs or a blog post, and run every example. Then change one thing in each example to see what breaks.
  • Minutes 16 to 20, tiny challenge. Solve one small problem on your own, even if it's just printing a pattern or reversing a string.

On weekends, swap the routine for a longer project session, maybe an hour, where you build something you care about. Projects are where scattered facts turn into real ability.

A few honest warnings. First, don't make your streak sacred. Missing a day is fine. What hurts is missing a week and deciding you've failed. If you slip, restart the next day with a five-minute session and carry on. Second, don't measure progress by hours spent. Measure it by what you can now do that you couldn't last month. Third, sleep. Memory gets filed overnight, and a tired brain makes the same bug feel impossible.

Seven Projects You Can Build Without a Laptop

Projects are the fastest way to learn JavaScript, because they force you to combine ideas and fix real problems. Every one of these works in the HirenJS editor on a phone. Start with the first, and move down the list as you grow.

1. GST and discount calculator

This one is useful in everyday life, which makes it motivating. Take a price, apply a discount, add GST, and print the final amount.

function finalPrice(price, discountPercent, gstPercent) {
  const discounted = price - (price * discountPercent) / 100;
  const withGst = discounted + (discounted * gstPercent) / 100;
  return Math.round(withGst * 100) / 100;
}

console.log(finalPrice(1000, 10, 18)); // 1062

Stretch goal: accept a list of items and print a total for the whole bill.

2. Number guessing game

The computer picks a secret number and you try to find it. You'll practise random numbers, conditions and functions.

const secret = Math.floor(Math.random() * 100) + 1;
let tries = 0;

function guess(n) {
  tries++;
  if (n === secret) {
    return `Correct! You needed ${tries} tries.`;
  }
  return n < secret ? 'Too low, try higher.' : 'Too high, try lower.';
}

console.log(guess(50));
console.log(guess(75));

Stretch goal: limit the player to seven guesses, then reveal the answer.

3. Temperature converter

Convert Celsius to Fahrenheit and back. It's tiny, but it teaches you to separate logic into functions and to format output neatly.

4. A simple to-do list

Switch to HTML mode. Add a text input, an Add button, and a list. When the button is tapped, create a new list item with the typed text. This is your first real taste of DOM manipulation, and it's a project that genuinely feels like an app.

<input id="task" placeholder="New task">
<button id="add">Add</button>
<ul id="list"></ul>

<script>
  const input = document.getElementById('task');
  const list = document.getElementById('list');

  document.getElementById('add').addEventListener('click', () => {
    const text = input.value.trim();
    if (!text) return;
    const li = document.createElement('li');
    li.textContent = text;
    list.appendChild(li);
    input.value = '';
  });
</script>

Stretch goal: tap an item to cross it out, then add a delete button.

5. Multiple-choice quiz

Store questions in an array of objects, show one at a time, and keep score. You'll use arrays, objects, loops, conditions and the DOM together. It's an excellent checkpoint project because it touches nearly everything from the roadmap.

6. Password strength checker

Check a password's length and whether it contains numbers, uppercase letters and symbols, then report "weak", "medium" or "strong". You'll practise strings, regular expressions at a basic level, and combining conditions.

7. Expense tracker

Keep an array of expenses with a category and an amount, then show totals per category. This is a great reason to use reduce, and it's something you could genuinely use to track your own spending. Once it works, add data that survives a refresh using the browser's local storage.

Whichever you pick, follow a simple routine. Write down in plain English what the program should do. Break it into the smallest steps you can. Build step one, test it, then move to step two. When a project feels too big, shrink it until the first piece is something you can finish in one sitting.

Common Mistakes and How to Avoid Them

After watching how learners get stuck, a handful of patterns come up again and again. Spot them early and you'll save yourself weeks.

Copy-pasting without understanding

It's tempting to paste an example, see it work and move on. But if you can't explain a line, you haven't learned it. A better habit is to type every example by hand, even on a phone. Typing forces your brain to process each character, and it's how you start noticing patterns in syntax.

Jumping between tutorials

"Tutorial hopping" feels productive, because each new video starts with exciting energy. In reality you keep re-learning the easy first lessons and never reach the hard, rewarding middle. Pick one learning path, such as the roadmap above, and stay with it until you've built something.

Ignoring error messages

Beginners often see red text and panic. Try reframing it. An error message is the computer telling you exactly where it got confused. Read it slowly. It usually names the problem and the line. We'll cover this more in the debugging section below.

Starting with a framework too early

React, Vue and the rest are powerful, but they assume you already understand functions, arrays, objects, scope and asynchronous code. If you jump in early, you'll end up memorising patterns you don't understand. Get the fundamentals solid first. Frameworks will then feel like a natural next step instead of magic.

Chasing perfect code

Your first versions will be messy, and that's completely normal. Get it working, then make it tidy. Experienced developers rewrite their own code constantly. Nobody writes it perfectly the first time.

Comparing yourself to others

Someone online will always seem faster. They might have studied for years before posting, or have a laptop, a mentor and unlimited free time. Compare yourself with who you were last month. That's the only comparison that's fair.

Giving up at the confusing parts

Closures, this, promises and async/await confuse almost everyone at first. Confusion isn't a sign you're not cut out for it. It's what learning feels like right before something clicks. When you hit a wall, step away, sleep on it, then try a much simpler example of the same idea.

How to Debug JavaScript on a Smartphone

Debugging means finding and fixing problems in your code, and it's a bigger part of programming than most beginners expect. The good news: you can do most of it without any special tools.

Read the error like a sentence

Most JavaScript errors follow the same shape: a type of error, a short message, and often a line number. Here are the three you'll meet constantly.

  • SyntaxError. You wrote something JavaScript can't parse, like a missing bracket, a missing quote or a stray comma. Check the line mentioned and the line above it.
  • ReferenceError. You used a name that doesn't exist, often through a typo or because the variable lives in a different scope. coutn instead of count is a classic.
  • TypeError. You tried to do something to a value that doesn't support it, like calling a function that is actually undefined, or reading a property of null.

Use console.log like a flashlight

If you don't know what a variable holds at a certain moment, print it. Add console.log('here 1') markers to see which parts of your code actually run, and print values before and after the line you suspect. It's simple, it works on every device, and professionals use it too.

function average(list) {
  console.log('input:', list);
  const total = list.reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0);
  console.log('total:', total);
  return total / list.length;
}

console.log(average([4, 8, 12]));

Shrink the problem

When a program of fifty lines misbehaves, copy it into a fresh editor and delete everything that isn't needed to reproduce the bug. Very often the bug becomes obvious halfway through deleting. If it doesn't, you now have a tiny, clear example you can share with someone else.

Check the boring things first

Before assuming something deep is wrong, check spelling and capitalisation, matching brackets and quotes, a forgotten return, and whether you used = (assign) where you meant === (compare). A surprising share of bugs are exactly this dull.

Explain it out loud

Programmers call it rubber duck debugging. Explain your code, line by line, to an imaginary listener. The act of putting your logic into words exposes the place where reality and your assumption part ways. It's silly and it works.

Take a break

If you've stared at the same bug for forty minutes, stop. Walk around, drink water, and come back. Fresh eyes spot in thirty seconds what tired eyes missed for an hour.

How to Ask for Help So People Actually Answer

Everyone gets stuck, and asking for help is a skill. A good question gets a quick, kind answer. A vague one gets silence. Here's a format that works almost everywhere, including in our community.

  1. Say what you're trying to do. One sentence is enough: "I want the button to add a new item to the list."
  2. Say what you expected and what happened. "I expected a new item to appear. Nothing appears and there's no error."
  3. Share the smallest code that shows the problem. Use the Share button in HirenJS and send the link. That way helpers can run your exact code in one tap.
  4. Say what you already tried. It shows effort and saves people from suggesting the same thing twice.
  5. Be patient and say thanks. When someone helps, tell them if it worked. It encourages them to help the next person.

Also, try to write your question as if the reader has no idea what's in your head. Something like "my code doesn't work" is almost impossible to answer, while "this loop prints 1 to 4 but I wanted 1 to 5" is easy.

Being Part of the HirenJS Community

A tool is only as good as the people using it. HirenJS began as a personal project, but it grows through feedback from learners, and I want it to feel like a shared space, not a one-way website. Here are practical ways you can take part, whether you're a complete beginner or already comfortable with code.

If you're a beginner

  • Tell us which topics confuse you most. Those are the posts we write next.
  • Report anything that feels clumsy on your phone. Small usability problems are exactly the ones a desktop developer wouldn't notice.
  • Share your finished mini projects. Seeing what others built is wonderful motivation.

If you already know some JavaScript

  • Help a beginner by looking at their shared link and pointing them in the right direction, without simply handing over the answer.
  • Suggest snippets or examples that taught you something. Good teaching examples are rarer than you'd think.
  • Spot a mistake in a tutorial? Tell us. Corrections make the blog better for everyone.

If you're a teacher or mentor

  • Use shared links to hand out exercises. Students open a link, and the starter code is already there.
  • Tell us what your students struggle with so we can improve the docs and quizzes.

For everyone

  • Follow the project on GitHub to see what's being built and when.
  • Pass HirenJS to one friend who says "I wish I could learn to code but I don't have a laptop." That sentence is the reason this site exists.

A few community habits I'd love us to keep. Be kind about questions, especially the basic ones, because everyone was new once. Give credit when you build on someone else's idea. And remember that explaining something to another person is one of the best ways to understand it yourself.

What's Next for HirenJS

When we launched version 2, I mentioned a few ideas that were on the table: a collaborative mode, more snippets and a small built-in debugger. They're still the direction I care about, because they all serve the same goal of making mobile coding feel less like a compromise. I'm not going to promise dates, because I'd rather ship things that work than announce things that aren't ready. What I can promise is that your feedback shapes the order.

On the content side, expect more tutorials aimed at the stages in the roadmap above: more on DOM projects, more small practice challenges, and plain-language explanations of the topics learners find hardest. If there's one you'd like to see sooner, let us know.

Choosing an Online JavaScript Editor for Your Phone

There are plenty of online JavaScript editors, and not all of them behave well on a small screen. Before you commit to one, run a quick test. Open it on your phone and check a few things. Does the code area resize properly when the keyboard appears, or does the keyboard cover the line you're typing? Are the Run and Undo buttons easy to reach with one thumb? Can you select and move the cursor precisely without zooming? Does it keep your code if you accidentally switch apps?

A good mobile-friendly JavaScript playground also keeps the interface calm. Too many panels, ads jumping around, or pop-ups covering the editor turn a twenty-minute session into a frustrating one. That's the reason HirenJS uses a dark, focused layout with the important actions at the bottom of the screen, within easy thumb reach. If you try other editors too, that's completely fine. Use whichever one lets you write code with the least friction. The best tool is the one you'll actually open every day.

What Can You Build with JavaScript?

It helps to know where the road leads. JavaScript started as a small language for adding behaviour to web pages, and it has grown into one of the most widely used languages in the world. On the front end, it powers the interactive parts of websites: menus, forms, animations, games, dashboards and charts. With tools like Node.js, the same language runs on servers, so you can build the back end of an app without learning a second language. People also use JavaScript for mobile apps, browser extensions, automation scripts and even small desktop programs.

You won't touch most of that in your first three months, and that's fine. The point is that the fundamentals you learn on your phone today are not a toy version. They're the exact same JavaScript used by professional developers. A loop is a loop whether it runs in a phone playground or a company's production code. Every skill you build now carries forward.

Learn JavaScript on Your Phone Without Burning Out

Motivation is easy on day one and surprisingly hard on day twenty. If you want to learn JavaScript on your phone and still be going three months from now, plan for the low-energy days instead of pretending they won't come.

Make the starting bar tiny. On a tired evening, the goal isn't "study for an hour." It's "open the editor and run one line." Most of the time, once you've started, you'll keep going. And on the days you don't, you've still kept the habit alive.

Celebrate small wins on purpose. The first time a loop prints the right numbers, the first time you fix an error without help, the first time your button actually responds, notice it. Write it in your notes app if you like. Looking back at that list on a discouraging day is a great reminder that you're moving forward.

Mix the types of practice. If you only read, you'll feel like you're learning without actually building skill. If you only code, you may repeat the same mistakes without understanding them. Alternate between reading a little, writing a little and reviewing a little. Variety keeps your mind engaged and strengthens memory.

Finally, find a study buddy if you can. Learning alongside a friend, a classmate or someone in the community makes it easier to show up, because someone's expecting you. Trade shared links, compare solutions to the same problem, and explain concepts to each other. Both of you improve faster than either would alone.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can I really learn JavaScript on my phone with no laptop?

Yes. JavaScript runs inside every modern mobile browser, so you can write and run code right on your phone using a JavaScript playground like HirenJS. A laptop becomes useful later for larger projects, but it isn't required to learn the language and build real mini projects.

Do I need an account or to install anything?

No. You open the site in your browser and start typing. You don't need to sign up to run code or to use the Share button.

How long does it take to learn JavaScript for beginners?

It depends on your time and consistency, but with 20 to 30 minutes a day, the 12-week roadmap above takes you from your first console.log to a small interactive project. Becoming truly confident takes longer, often six months to a year of regular practice. Be wary of anyone promising mastery in a few days.

Is my code saved if I close the browser?

HirenJS auto-saves your code in your browser as you type, so it's normally still there when you return. Browsers can clear stored data, though, so for anything important, press Share and keep the link in your notes as a backup.

Can I practise HTML and CSS here too?

Yes. HTML mode includes a live preview, so you can build small pages, style them and connect them to JavaScript. That's the best way to see your code do something visible.

Should I learn Python or JavaScript first?

Both are good first languages. JavaScript has one big advantage for phone-only learners: it runs in the browser you already have, with no setup, and it lets you see results on a real web page quickly. If your goal is anything to do with websites, JavaScript is a natural starting point.

Can learning JavaScript lead to a job?

It can, but I want to be realistic. JavaScript is widely used for building websites and apps, so the skill is valuable. A job usually needs more than the language itself: projects you can show, comfort with HTML, CSS and tools like Git, and time. This guide gets you started well. It doesn't replace the long road after it.

What should I do when I'm stuck?

Read the error message, print values with console.log, shrink the problem, and take a short break. If you're still stuck, share your code link along with what you expected and what happened. Clear questions get quick answers.

How do I know I'm making progress?

Try this test every month: pick a small problem, like reversing a string or summing a list, and solve it without help. If you can do something this month that felt impossible last month, you're progressing, even if it doesn't feel like it day to day.

Your First Step Starts Today

You don't need the perfect device, the perfect plan or a long free evening. You need a phone, a browser and twenty honest minutes. Open the editor, type console.log('Hello, world!'), press Run, and watch your first line of JavaScript work. That small moment is the start of everything else.

If you've read this far, you already have more patience than many people who try to learn JavaScript on their phone, and patience is the quality that matters most. Pick one section of the roadmap, set a timer, and begin. Come back to this guide whenever you need it. Tell us what you build. And if you get stuck, send us a link and say what you were trying to do.

Happy coding, and welcome to the HirenJS community.

title: JavaScript Promises Explained Step by Step
excerpt: Promises are the foundation of async JavaScript. Learn pending, fulfilled and rejected states with small examples you can run on your phone.
author: Hiren Rathod
content:
A Promise is an object that represents a value you don't have yet, but will get in the future. Think of it like ordering food: you get a token now, and the food arrives later (or the order gets cancelled).

The 3 States

Every promise is in one of three states: pending (waiting), fulfilled (success) or rejected (failed). Once it moves out of pending, it never changes again.

Creating a Promise

const order = new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
  setTimeout(() => {
    const ok = true;
    if (ok) resolve('Pizza delivered');
    else reject('Order cancelled');
  }, 1000);
});

order
  .then(msg => console.log(msg))
  .catch(err => console.error(err))
  .finally(() => console.log('Done'));

Chaining

Every .then() returns a new promise, so you can chain steps one after another.

Promise.resolve(5)
  .then(n => n * 2)
  .then(n => n + 1)
  .then(result => console.log(result)); // 11

Useful Helpers

Promise.all([p1, p2, p3]);        // wait for all, fail if any fails
Promise.allSettled([p1, p2, p3]); // wait for all, never fails
Promise.race([p1, p2]);           // first one to finish wins

Paste these into HirenJS, change ok to false and see how the catch block runs.

title: Destructuring in JavaScript: Write Less, Do More
excerpt: Pull values out of arrays and objects in one line. Destructuring makes your code shorter and much easier to read.
author: Hiren Rathod
content:
Destructuring is a shortcut to unpack values from arrays or properties from objects into separate variables.

Array Destructuring

const colors = ['red', 'green', 'blue'];
const [first, second] = colors;
console.log(first, second); // red green

// skip items
const [, , third] = colors;
console.log(third); // blue

Object Destructuring

const user = { name: 'Arjun', age: 21, city: 'Surat' };
const { name, city } = user;
console.log(name, city); // Arjun Surat

// rename + default value
const { age: years, country = 'India' } = user;
console.log(years, country); // 21 India

In Function Parameters

function greet({ name, city = 'Unknown' }) {
  return `Hello ${name} from ${city}`;
}
console.log(greet({ name: 'Priya' })); // Hello Priya from Unknown

Swapping Variables

let a = 1, b = 2;
[a, b] = [b, a];
console.log(a, b); // 2 1

Once you start using destructuring, you will not want to go back to user.name, user.city everywhere.

title: Spread and Rest Operators: The Three Dots Explained
excerpt: Same three dots, two different jobs. Learn when ... expands and when it collects.
author: Hiren Rathod
content:
The ... syntax looks the same everywhere, but it does two opposite things depending on where you use it.

Spread: Expand Things

const a = [1, 2, 3];
const b = [...a, 4, 5];
console.log(b); // [1,2,3,4,5]

const base = { theme: 'dark', size: 14 };
const custom = { ...base, size: 18 };
console.log(custom); // { theme: 'dark', size: 18 }

Spread makes a shallow copy. Nested objects are still shared, so be careful.

Rest: Collect Things

function sum(...numbers) {
  return numbers.reduce((t, n) => t + n, 0);
}
console.log(sum(1, 2, 3, 4)); // 10

const [head, ...others] = [10, 20, 30, 40];
console.log(head, others); // 10 [20,30,40]

Easy Rule

If the dots are where values are given (calling a function, building an array), it is spread. If they are where values are received (function parameters, destructuring), it is rest.

title: Arrow Functions vs Normal Functions (and the this Keyword)
excerpt: Arrow functions are shorter, but they also behave differently with this. Know exactly when to use which.
author: Hiren Rathod
content:
Arrow functions came with ES6 and give a shorter syntax. But the real difference is how they treat this.

Syntax

// normal
function add(a, b) { return a + b; }

// arrow
const add2 = (a, b) => a + b;

// single parameter, no brackets needed
const square = n => n * n;

The this Difference

A normal function gets its own this depending on how it is called. An arrow function does not have its own this, it uses the one from the surrounding code.

const timer = {
  seconds: 0,
  startBad() {
    setTimeout(function () {
      console.log(this.seconds); // undefined (this is not timer)
    }, 100);
  },
  startGood() {
    setTimeout(() => {
      console.log(this.seconds); // 0 (this is timer)
    }, 100);
  }
};
timer.startBad();
timer.startGood();

When NOT to Use Arrows

Do not use arrow functions as object methods or constructors. Use them for callbacks like map, filter and setTimeout.

title: DOM Manipulation Basics: Select, Change, Create
excerpt: The DOM is how JavaScript talks to a web page. Learn the five operations you will use in every project.
author: Hiren Rathod
content:
The DOM (Document Object Model) is the page represented as objects. With JavaScript you can read it, change it and add new elements.

1. Selecting Elements

const title = document.querySelector('h1');
const items = document.querySelectorAll('.item');

2. Changing Content

title.textContent = 'Hello HirenJS';
title.style.color = 'orange';
title.classList.add('highlight');

3. Creating Elements

const li = document.createElement('li');
li.textContent = 'New item';
document.querySelector('ul').appendChild(li);

4. Removing Elements

li.remove();

5. Attributes

const link = document.querySelector('a');
link.setAttribute('href', 'https://hiren.js.org');
console.log(link.getAttribute('href'));

Tip: prefer textContent over innerHTML when showing user input. It prevents script injection bugs.

Switch HirenJS to HTML mode and try these in the live preview.

title: Event Listeners and Event Delegation Made Simple
excerpt: Click, input, keydown: handle user actions the right way, and learn the delegation trick that saves dozens of listeners.
author: Hiren Rathod
content:
Events are things that happen on a page: clicks, typing, scrolling. You react to them with addEventListener.

Basic Listener

const btn = document.querySelector('#btn');
btn.addEventListener('click', (e) => {
  console.log('Clicked!', e.target);
});

The Event Object

The callback receives an event object. Useful properties: e.target (what was clicked), e.key (keyboard), e.preventDefault() (stop default behaviour like form submit).

Event Delegation

Instead of adding a listener to every list item, add one to the parent. Events bubble up, so the parent can catch them all, even for items added later.

const list = document.querySelector('ul');
list.addEventListener('click', (e) => {
  if (e.target.matches('li')) {
    e.target.classList.toggle('done');
  }
});

Removing a Listener

function onClick() { console.log('hi'); }
btn.addEventListener('click', onClick);
btn.removeEventListener('click', onClick);

Delegation is the pattern behind every todo app. Build one in HirenJS to practise.

title: localStorage: Save Data in the Browser
excerpt: Make your apps remember things. A practical guide to localStorage with a working todo-saving example.
author: Hiren Rathod
content:
localStorage lets you store key-value pairs in the browser. Data stays even after you close the tab.

The 4 Methods

localStorage.setItem('theme', 'dark');
console.log(localStorage.getItem('theme')); // dark
localStorage.removeItem('theme');
localStorage.clear(); // removes everything

Only Strings Allowed

localStorage stores only strings. To save arrays or objects, convert them with JSON.stringify and back with JSON.parse.

const todos = [{ text: 'Learn JS', done: false }];
localStorage.setItem('todos', JSON.stringify(todos));

const saved = JSON.parse(localStorage.getItem('todos')) || [];
console.log(saved);

Safe Helper

function load(key, fallback) {
  try {
    return JSON.parse(localStorage.getItem(key)) ?? fallback;
  } catch {
    return fallback;
  }
}

Limits

You get around 5 MB per site. Never store passwords or tokens in it, because any script on the page can read it.

title: Fetch API and JSON: Get Data from the Internet
excerpt: Learn to call APIs with fetch, read JSON responses and handle errors properly.
author: Hiren Rathod
content:
Almost every modern app talks to an API. In the browser you do this with fetch.

GET Request

async function getUsers() {
  const res = await fetch('https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/users');
  if (!res.ok) throw new Error('HTTP ' + res.status);
  const users = await res.json();
  console.log(users.map(u => u.name));
}
getUsers().catch(console.error);

Important: fetch does not throw on 404 or 500. You must check res.ok yourself.

POST Request

async function createPost() {
  const res = await fetch('https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/posts', {
    method: 'POST',
    headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' },
    body: JSON.stringify({ title: 'Hello', body: 'From HirenJS', userId: 1 })
  });
  console.log(await res.json());
}
createPost();

What is JSON?

JSON is a text format for data. Keys must be in double quotes and there are no functions or comments. Use JSON.parse() to text-to-object and JSON.stringify() for object-to-text.

title: JavaScript Classes and OOP for Beginners
excerpt: Classes, constructors, inheritance and private fields explained with a simple Vehicle example.
author: Hiren Rathod
content:
A class is a blueprint for creating objects with the same structure and behaviour.

Your First Class

class Vehicle {
  constructor(name, speed) {
    this.name = name;
    this.speed = speed;
  }
  describe() {
    return `${this.name} runs at ${this.speed} km/h`;
  }
}

const bike = new Vehicle('Bike', 80);
console.log(bike.describe());

Inheritance

class Car extends Vehicle {
  constructor(name, speed, doors) {
    super(name, speed);
    this.doors = doors;
  }
  describe() {
    return super.describe() + ` with ${this.doors} doors`;
  }
}

console.log(new Car('Swift', 160, 4).describe());

Private Fields and Static Methods

class Wallet {
  #balance = 0;
  static currency = 'INR';
  add(n) { this.#balance += n; }
  get balance() { return this.#balance; }
}

const w = new Wallet();
w.add(500);
console.log(w.balance, Wallet.currency);

The # prefix makes a field truly private. Nobody outside the class can touch it.

title: ES6 Modules: import and export Explained
excerpt: Split your code into clean files. Learn named exports, default exports and common mistakes.
author: Hiren Rathod
content:
As projects grow, one giant file becomes painful. Modules let you split code into files and share only what you want.

Named Exports

// math.js
export const PI = 3.14159;
export function area(r) { return PI * r * r; }

// app.js
import { PI, area } from './math.js';
console.log(area(5));

Default Export

// logger.js
export default function log(msg) {
  console.log('[LOG]', msg);
}

// app.js
import log from './logger.js';
log('Hello');

Rename and Import Everything

import { area as circleArea } from './math.js';
import * as MathUtils from './math.js';
console.log(MathUtils.PI);

Using Modules in HTML

<script type="module" src="app.js"></script>

Remember: modules need a server (even a simple local one). Opening the file directly with file:// will usually give a CORS error.

title: Debugging Like a Pro: Beyond console.log
excerpt: console.table, console.group, console.time and more. Find bugs faster with the tools already in your browser.
author: Hiren Rathod
content:
Most beginners only know console.log. The console has many more methods that save hours.

console.table()

const students = [
  { name: 'Arjun', score: 85 },
  { name: 'Priya', score: 92 }
];
console.table(students);

console.group()

console.group('User Info');
console.log('Name: Hiren');
console.log('City: Gujarat');
console.groupEnd();

console.time()

console.time('loop');
for (let i = 0; i < 1000000; i++) {}
console.timeEnd('loop');

console.error and console.warn

Use these to separate real problems from normal logs. They show in different colours and are easy to filter.

The debugger Keyword

function calc(a, b) {
  debugger; // pauses here if DevTools is open
  return a + b;
}

Bonus habit: when something breaks, log the type as well: console.log(typeof value, value). Half of all bugs are the wrong type.

title: The JavaScript Event Loop in Plain Language
excerpt: Why does setTimeout(0) run last? Understand the call stack, task queue and microtasks once and for all.
author: Hiren Rathod
content:
JavaScript has one thread, yet it handles timers, network calls and clicks without freezing. The secret is the event loop.

The Pieces

Call stack: where your code runs, one function at a time. Web APIs: the browser handles timers and network outside the stack. Task queue: callbacks (like setTimeout) wait here. Microtask queue: promise callbacks wait here, with higher priority.

Guess the Output

console.log('1');

setTimeout(() => console.log('2'), 0);

Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log('3'));

console.log('4');

The answer is 1, 4, 3, 2. Synchronous code runs first (1, 4). Then the event loop empties the microtask queue (3) before taking the next task (2).

Why Heavy Loops Freeze the Page

If the call stack is busy, the event loop cannot run anything else. A long for loop blocks clicks and rendering. Break big work into small chunks or use Web Workers.

Run the example in HirenJS, then add more logs and predict the order before running.

title: Callbacks and Higher-Order Functions Demystified
excerpt: Functions that take or return other functions are everywhere in JavaScript. Learn the idea once, use it forever.
author: Hiren Rathod
content:
In JavaScript, functions are values. You can store them in variables, pass them to other functions and return them. A function that does this is called a higher-order function.

Passing a Function (Callback)

function repeat(times, action) {
  for (let i = 0; i < times; i++) action(i);
}

repeat(3, (i) => console.log('Run number', i));

Returning a Function

function multiplier(factor) {
  return (n) => n * factor;
}

const double = multiplier(2);
const triple = multiplier(3);
console.log(double(10), triple(10)); // 20 30

You Already Use Them

map, filter, reduce, forEach, setTimeout and addEventListener are all higher-order functions that accept callbacks.

Build Your Own filter

function myFilter(arr, test) {
  const result = [];
  for (const item of arr) {
    if (test(item)) result.push(item);
  }
  return result;
}
console.log(myFilter([1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6], n => n % 2 === 0)); // [2,4,6]

title: JavaScript String Methods Cheat Sheet
excerpt: slice, split, replace, includes, padStart and more. The string methods you will actually use, with examples.
author: Hiren Rathod
content:
Strings are everywhere: usernames, URLs, messages. Here are the methods worth remembering.

Search and Check

const s = 'Learn JavaScript on HirenJS';
console.log(s.includes('Java'));   // true
console.log(s.startsWith('Learn')); // true
console.log(s.indexOf('on'));      // 17

Extract

console.log(s.slice(0, 5));  // Learn
console.log(s.split(' '));   // ['Learn','JavaScript','on','HirenJS']

Change

console.log(s.toUpperCase());
console.log(s.replace('Learn', 'Master'));
console.log('  spaces  '.trim()); // 'spaces'
console.log('ha'.repeat(3));     // hahaha

Formatting

console.log('7'.padStart(2, '0')); // 07
const name = 'Priya';
console.log(`Hello ${name}!`);     // template literal

Remember

Strings are immutable. Methods never change the original, they return a new string. Always save the result in a variable.

title: Working with Dates in JavaScript Without Pain
excerpt: The Date object has strange behaviour. Learn the safe way to create, format and compare dates.
author: Hiren Rathod
content:
Dates look simple, but they have traps. Let's learn the safe parts.

Creating Dates

const now = new Date();
const d = new Date('2026-10-06');
const custom = new Date(2026, 9, 6); // month starts from 0! 9 = October
console.log(now.getFullYear(), custom.getMonth());

Formatting for Indian Users

const date = new Date('2026-10-06');
console.log(date.toLocaleDateString('en-IN', {
  day: 'numeric', month: 'long', year: 'numeric'
})); // 6 October 2026

Comparing and Calculating

const a = new Date('2026-01-01');
const b = new Date('2026-03-01');
const days = (b - a) / (1000 * 60 * 60 * 24);
console.log(days); // 59

Adding Days

function addDays(date, n) {
  const copy = new Date(date);
  copy.setDate(copy.getDate() + n);
  return copy;
}
console.log(addDays(new Date('2026-10-06'), 10));

Biggest trap: months are zero-based (0 = January) but days are one-based. Also always use ISO format YYYY-MM-DD when creating from strings.

title: Error Handling in JavaScript: try, catch and Custom Errors
excerpt: Stop your app from crashing. Learn try/catch/finally, throwing errors and creating your own error types.
author: Hiren Rathod
content:
Errors will happen: bad input, network failure, missing data. Good developers plan for them.

try / catch / finally

try {
  const data = JSON.parse('{ bad json }');
} catch (err) {
  console.error('Parsing failed:', err.message);
} finally {
  console.log('This always runs');
}

Throwing Your Own Errors

function divide(a, b) {
  if (b === 0) throw new Error('Cannot divide by zero');
  return a / b;
}

try {
  divide(10, 0);
} catch (e) {
  console.log(e.message);
}

Custom Error Classes

class ValidationError extends Error {
  constructor(field, message) {
    super(message);
    this.name = 'ValidationError';
    this.field = field;
  }
}

try {
  throw new ValidationError('email', 'Email is invalid');
} catch (e) {
  if (e instanceof ValidationError) {
    console.log(e.field + ': ' + e.message);
  }
}

Rule of Thumb

Catch errors only where you can do something useful about them, like showing a message to the user. Do not swallow them silently with an empty catch block.

title: 7 Common JavaScript Mistakes Every Beginner Makes
excerpt: == vs ===, forgetting await, mutating arrays and more. Avoid these and you will save hours of debugging.
author: Hiren Rathod
content:
Every developer made these mistakes. Knowing them early saves a lot of frustration.

1. Using == Instead of ===

console.log(0 == '0');  // true (confusing)
console.log(0 === '0'); // false (clear)

2. Forgetting await

const res = fetch(url);        // Promise, not data!
const res2 = await fetch(url); // correct

3. Comparing Objects and Arrays

console.log([1,2] === [1,2]); // false, different references

4. Modifying an Array While Looping

Removing items inside a for loop shifts indexes and skips elements. Use filter() to create a new array instead.

5. Using var in Loops with Callbacks

for (var i = 0; i < 3; i++) setTimeout(() => console.log(i)); // 3 3 3
for (let j = 0; j < 3; j++) setTimeout(() => console.log(j)); // 0 1 2

6. Trusting typeof null

console.log(typeof null); // 'object' (an old JS bug)

7. Floating Point Surprises

console.log(0.1 + 0.2); // 0.30000000000000004
console.log((0.1 + 0.2).toFixed(2)); // '0.30'

Try each one in HirenJS and see the output yourself. Seeing the bug once is the best way to remember it.

title: 5 Mini Projects to Learn JavaScript Faster
excerpt: Tutorials are not enough. Build these five small projects and your JavaScript skills will grow quickly.
author: Hiren Rathod
content:
Watching tutorials feels productive, but real learning happens when you build. Here are five small projects, each teaching a different skill.

1. Counter App

Buttons to increase, decrease and reset a number. Teaches DOM selection, events and updating text.

2. Todo List with Saving

Add, delete and mark tasks done. Save everything to localStorage. Teaches arrays, event delegation and JSON.

3. Random Quote Generator

Show a new quote on each click, first from an array, then from a public API. Teaches fetch and async/await.

4. Simple Calculator

Buttons for digits and operators with a display. Teaches functions, state and handling edge cases like dividing by zero.

5. Quiz Game

Questions stored as objects, track score, show result at the end.

const questions = [
  { q: 'Which keyword declares a constant?', options: ['var', 'let', 'const'], answer: 2 },
  { q: 'What does === check?', options: ['value only', 'value and type'], answer: 1 }
];
let score = 0;
questions.forEach(item => {
  // show question, read the choice, then:
  // if (choice === item.answer) score++;
});

How to Practise

Build the first version ugly and working. Then improve it one feature at a time. Even 30 minutes a day on a phone adds up fast.

title: JavaScript Closures Explained for Beginners
excerpt: Closures are one of the most powerful and misunderstood concepts in JavaScript. In this guide we break them down with real examples you can run right in HirenJS.
author: Hiren Rathod
content:
A closure is a function that remembers the variables from the place where it was created, even after that outer function has finished running. This sounds confusing at first, but once it clicks, you'll see closures everywhere in JavaScript.

What is a Closure?

Every time you create a function inside another function, the inner function forms a closure. It holds a reference to the outer function's variables — even after the outer function returns.

function makeCounter() {
  let count = 0;  // this variable is 'closed over'
  return function() {
    count++;
    return count;
  };
}

const counter = makeCounter();
console.log(counter()); // 1
console.log(counter()); // 2
console.log(counter()); // 3

Notice that count persists between calls. The inner function has a reference to count in its closure — it's not a copy, it's the actual variable.

Why Are Closures Useful?

Closures let you create private variables — data that only the inner function can access and modify. This is a fundamental pattern for data encapsulation in JavaScript.

function createBankAccount(initialBalance) {
  let balance = initialBalance; // private!

  return {
    deposit(amount) { balance += amount; },
    withdraw(amount) {
      if (amount > balance) return 'Insufficient funds';
      balance -= amount;
    },
    getBalance() { return balance; }
  };
}

const account = createBankAccount(1000);
account.deposit(500);
console.log(account.getBalance()); // 1500
console.log(account.balance);      // undefined — it's private!

Closures in the Real World

You use closures constantly in modern JavaScript — in React hooks, event listeners, setTimeout callbacks, and module patterns. Understanding closures makes all of these click into place.

Try It in HirenJS

Open the HirenJS editor and paste these examples in. Experiment with modifying the counter or bank account to build your intuition. The best way to understand closures is to break them and fix them!

title: Top 10 Array Methods Every JS Developer Must Know
excerpt: From map() to reduce(), these array methods are the secret weapon of every productive JavaScript developer. Master them and your code will never be the same.
author: Hiren Rathod
content:
Arrays are the most used data structure in JavaScript. Knowing the right method for the right job makes your code cleaner, shorter, and easier to understand. Here are the 10 array methods you'll use every single day.

1. map() — Transform Every Element

Returns a new array where every element has been transformed by a function.

const prices = [10, 20, 30];
const withTax = prices.map(p => p * 1.18);
console.log(withTax); // [11.8, 23.6, 35.4]

2. filter() — Keep Only What Matches

Returns a new array containing only elements that pass a test.

const scores = [45, 78, 32, 90, 55, 88];
const passing = scores.filter(s => s >= 50);
console.log(passing); // [78, 90, 55, 88]

3. reduce() — Collapse to One Value

The most powerful array method. Reduces an array to a single value.

const cart = [299, 149, 89, 599];
const total = cart.reduce((sum, item) => sum + item, 0);
console.log(total); // 1136

4. find() — Get the First Match

const users = [{id:1,name:'Hiren'},{id:2,name:'Raj'}];
const user = users.find(u => u.id === 2);
console.log(user.name); // Raj

5. some() and every()

const nums = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5];
console.log(nums.some(n => n > 4));  // true
console.log(nums.every(n => n > 0)); // true

6. flat() and flatMap()

const nested = [[1,2],[3,4],[5,6]];
console.log(nested.flat()); // [1,2,3,4,5,6]

const sentences = ['Hello World', 'JS Rocks'];
const words = sentences.flatMap(s => s.split(' '));
console.log(words); // ['Hello','World','JS','Rocks']

7. sort() — with a Comparator

const items = [30, 1, 21, 8];
items.sort((a, b) => a - b); // ascending
console.log(items); // [1, 8, 21, 30]

8. includes()

const fruits = ['mango','apple','banana'];
console.log(fruits.includes('apple')); // true

9. Array.from()

// Create array of 5 zeros
const zeros = Array.from({length: 5}, () => 0);
console.log(zeros); // [0,0,0,0,0]

// Numbers 1-10
const oneToTen = Array.from({length:10}, (_,i) => i+1);
console.log(oneToTen);

10. Chaining Them Together

The real power comes from chaining these methods:

const students = [
  {name:'Arjun', score:85},
  {name:'Priya', score:42},
  {name:'Rahul', score:91},
  {name:'Meena', score:38},
];

const topStudents = students
  .filter(s => s.score >= 50)
  .sort((a,b) => b.score - a.score)
  .map(s => `${s.name}: ${s.score}`);

console.log(topStudents);
// ['Rahul: 91', 'Arjun: 85']

Practice all of these in HirenJS — copy each snippet, run it, then modify the data to see how the output changes.

title: Async/Await: The Complete Guide for Students
excerpt: Asynchronous JavaScript used to be painful. async/await makes it feel like normal code. Here's everything you need to know, with mobile-friendly examples.
author: Hiren Rathod
content:
JavaScript runs on a single thread — it can only do one thing at a time. But modern apps need to fetch data, read files, and wait for timers without freezing the page. async/await is how you handle this elegantly.

The Problem: Callbacks

// Old way — callback hell
getUser(id, function(user) {
  getPosts(user.id, function(posts) {
    getComments(posts[0].id, function(comments) {
      // deeply nested and hard to read!
    });
  });
});

The Evolution: Promises

getUser(id)
  .then(user => getPosts(user.id))
  .then(posts => getComments(posts[0].id))
  .then(comments => console.log(comments))
  .catch(err => console.error(err));

The Modern Way: async/await

async function loadData(id) {
  try {
    const user     = await getUser(id);
    const posts    = await getPosts(user.id);
    const comments = await getComments(posts[0].id);
    console.log(comments);
  } catch (err) {
    console.error('Something went wrong:', err);
  }
}

See how async/await reads like regular synchronous code? That's the whole point.

Real Example: Fetching from an API

async function getJoke() {
  const response = await fetch(
    'https://v2.jokeapi.dev/joke/Programming?type=single'
  );
  const data = await response.json();
  console.log('Joke:', data.joke);
}

getJoke();

Running Multiple Requests at Once

// Sequential — slow (one waits for the other)
const user  = await getUser(1);
const posts = await getPosts(1);

// Parallel — fast (both run at the same time!)
const [user, posts] = await Promise.all([
  getUser(1),
  getPosts(1)
]);

Use Promise.all() whenever your requests don't depend on each other — it can make your app significantly faster.

Error Handling

Always wrap async code in try/catch. Without it, unhandled promise rejections can silently break your app.

title: HirenJS v2 is Here — Everything That's New
excerpt: After months of work, HirenJS v2 launches with a complete redesign, 6 editor themes, snippet library, HTML preview mode, and a brand new mobile experience.
author: Hiren Rathod
content:
After months of building, testing on real student devices, and gathering feedback, HirenJS v2 is officially live. Here's a full rundown of everything that's changed.

Complete Visual Redesign

The entire UI has been rebuilt from scratch with a dark-first design that's easier on the eyes for long coding sessions. The new design uses a consistent colour system, better typography (JetBrains Mono for code, Syne for UI), and subtle animations that make the editor feel premium without being distracting.

6 Editor Themes

You can now cycle through six built-in Ace Editor themes: One Dark, Monokai, Dracula, GitHub, Night Bright, and Cobalt. Tap the Theme button in the toolbar or use the bottom bar on mobile.

Snippet Library

12 hand-crafted code snippets are now built in — from Hello World to Design Patterns. Open the snippet library with Ctrl+K, search for what you want, and the code is inserted instantly. Each snippet is written to teach a real concept, not just be a boilerplate.

HTML Preview Mode

Switch to HTML mode and the new Preview tab shows your HTML rendered live in a sandboxed iframe. Great for learning DOM manipulation and CSS without needing a separate editor.

Share Your Code via URL

The Share button encodes your code into a URL that anyone can open to see exactly what you wrote. No login, no account — just copy and send the link to your teacher or friend.

Mobile Bottom Toolbar

On phones, five essential actions now live in a fixed bottom bar: Run, Undo, Clear, Format, and Theme. The Run button is a large yellow circle — impossible to miss, even on a small screen.

Auto-Save

Your code is saved to localStorage automatically as you type. Close the tab, come back later — everything is still there.

What's Next?

We're working on a collaborative mode, more snippets, and a built-in mini debugger. Follow the project on GitHub to stay updated!

title: 5 Tips to Code Effectively on Your Smartphone
excerpt: Most students in India learn to code on a phone. Here are 5 practical tips to make mobile coding faster, smarter, and less frustrating.
author: Hiren Rathod
content:
Coding on a smartphone is genuinely possible — HirenJS was built specifically for it. But there are habits and tricks that make the experience dramatically better. Here are the five most impactful ones.

1. Use Landscape Mode for More Space

Rotating your phone to landscape gives you significantly more horizontal space for code. Most mobile editors, including HirenJS, lay out much better in landscape for writing. Switch to portrait to read output.

2. Use the Snippet Library as a Starting Point

Don't type boilerplate from scratch on a phone keyboard. In HirenJS, press the 📦 icon to open the snippet library. Find the pattern closest to what you need, insert it, then modify it. You'll type maybe 20% as much.

3. Learn the Mobile Bottom Bar

HirenJS's bottom toolbar puts Run, Undo, Format, and Theme one tap away. The Format button (✨) auto-indents your code — incredibly useful when phone keyboards mess up your spacing.

4. Use the Share Button to Save Your Work

Before closing your browser, hit 🔗 Share and copy the URL. Paste it in your notes app. If your browser clears localStorage, you still have your code in that link.

5. Write Short, Test Often

On a phone, it's harder to scroll through long files. The best habit is to write 5-10 lines, hit Run, check the output, then continue. This short feedback loop also makes debugging much easier — you always know which few lines caused the problem.

Bonus: Use a Bluetooth Keyboard

If you have access to a cheap Bluetooth keyboard (they're available for under ₹500), pairing it with your phone transforms the coding experience entirely. HirenJS has full keyboard shortcut support including Ctrl+Enter to run.

title: JavaScript Scope: Let, Const, Var and the Temporal Dead Zone
excerpt: Why does var behave so strangely? What's the Temporal Dead Zone? This deep-dive into JavaScript scope will answer questions you didn't even know you had.
author: Hiren Rathod
content:
Scope determines where variables are accessible in your code. JavaScript has three types of scope: global, function, and block. Understanding this is essential to avoiding bugs that are incredibly hard to trace.

var — Function Scoped (and Weird)

function example() {
  if (true) {
    var x = 10; // var is function-scoped, not block-scoped
  }
  console.log(x); // 10 — still accessible outside the if block!
}
example();

This surprises beginners. var leaks out of if, for, and while blocks — it only respects function boundaries.

let and const — Block Scoped

function betterExample() {
  if (true) {
    let y = 20;
    const z = 30;
  }
  console.log(y); // ReferenceError — y is not defined
}

let and const are block-scoped — they only exist inside the { } where they were declared.

Hoisting

JavaScript moves variable and function declarations to the top of their scope before executing. This is called hoisting.

console.log(name); // undefined (not an error!)
var name = 'Hiren';

// What JS actually does:
var name;
console.log(name); // undefined
name = 'Hiren';

The Temporal Dead Zone (TDZ)

let and const are also hoisted, but they're not initialised — accessing them before declaration throws a ReferenceError. The gap between the start of the block and the declaration is called the Temporal Dead Zone.

console.log(age); // ReferenceError: Cannot access 'age' before initialization
let age = 22;

The Rule

Always use const first. Use let only if you need to reassign. Never use var in new code. This simple rule prevents 90% of scope-related bugs.
